method: FP8-E4M3 scale quantization (NVFP4-style block scales)
source: NVIDIA NVFP4 (developer.nvidia.com/blog/introducing-nvfp4-for-efficient-and-accurate-low-precision-inference; docs.nvidia.com Transformer Engine NVFP4); QLoRA uses FP8 for constants (arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314)
mechanism: Round each f16 group scale to fp8-e4m3, plus one f32 per-tensor scale to renormalize dynamic range into e4m3's +/-448 (exactly NVFP4's hierarchical scale scheme, applied to our g128 1-bit groups instead of fp4 blocks). Kernels decode e4m3->f16 inline (few ALU ops or a 256-entry LUT).
training_free: YES — pure re-rounding of existing scales; no data, no gradients, no calibration.
inference_native: YES with a small kernel patch — the fp8 scale is what the qmm kernel reads. MLX mainline already decodes e4m3 scales in its nvfp4 mode, so the decode path exists to copy into the 1-bit affine kernel.
metal_feasible: YES, kernel-trivial in the patched MLX fork: swap the half scale load for a byte load + e4m3 decode. Precedent code in mlx nvfp4 mode.
est_savings: Scales 0.125->0.0625 bpw; saves 0.0625 bpw = 210.9 MB = 5.56% of the 3.797 GB model (50% of the 421.9 MB scale metadata). New total 1.0625 bpw.
notes: CONSTRAINT-CROSSING (rule 4): modifies stored scale values; max relative rounding error 2^-4 = 6.25% per scale (3 mantissa bits), typical RMS ~2-3%. In a 1-bit format every dequantized weight is sign*scale+bias, so scale error perturbs all 128 weights of the group directly — expect measurable within-format KL, must be benchmarked like a fold. Ceiling context: deleting ALL scale metadata caps at 11.1% of bytes. Caveat: stated format is f16 scale+bias per 128 (arithmetic 1.25 bpw, quoted 1.125) — if a separate f16 group bias exists, every method here applies to it identically and absolute savings double (~422 MB at 8-bit for scale+bias).

method: Double quantization of scales (QLoRA-style DQ: int8/fp8 scales + second-level f32 per 256 groups)
source: QLoRA, Dettmers et al. 2023, Sec. 'Double Quantization' (arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314); bitsandbytes implementation
mechanism: Treat the 210.9M f16 scales as a tensor; blockwise (256 scales/block) affine-quantize them to 8-bit after subtracting per-block min, keeping one f32 second-level scale (+min) per block. Kernel does a two-level dequant: fetch u8 scale, multiply by the block's f32 second-level constant.
training_free: YES — min/max statistics over existing scales only; QLoRA's DQ needs no calibration data.
inference_native: YES with kernel patch — bitsandbytes' 4-bit inference kernels consume DQ'd constants directly; same structure portable to MLX qmm (one extra scalar fetch per 256 groups, amortized to noise).
metal_feasible: YES, modest: add second-level constant buffer + one fused multiply in the 1-bit qmm kernel of the fork. llama.cpp proves two-level scale dequant runs fine in Metal.
est_savings: Scales 0.125->0.0635 bpw; saves 0.0615 bpw = 207.6 MB = 5.47% of model bytes. New total 1.0635 bpw. (QLoRA's quoted 0.373 bpw saving was for 4-bit g64 f32 scales; our f16 g128 baseline yields the smaller number.)
notes: CONSTRAINT-CROSSING: re-rounds scale values (256 levels per block; error small unless scales within a 256-group block span a huge range — check per-tensor scale histograms first, experiments/census). Slightly worse ratio than flat fp8 but better accuracy when scale distributions are wide, since the second level adapts per block. Same 1-bit sensitivity caveat as fp8 scales.

method: GGUF k-quant superblock scheme adapted to 1-bit (6-bit sub-scales + one f16 super-scale per 8 groups)
source: llama.cpp k-quants (Q4_K/Q6_K design; apxml.com GGUF format docs; zeroentropy.dev/concepts/gguf; kaitchup.substack.com k-quants guide)
mechanism: Group 8 consecutive g128 scales into a 1024-weight superblock; store one f16 super-scale (max) plus 6-bit integer sub-scales relative to it: s_i = q6_i * s_super/63. This is exactly Q4_K's double-quantized-scales trick with our group geometry.
training_free: YES — max + rounding over existing scales.
inference_native: YES — this is llama.cpp's shipping on-disk format; kernels consume it directly with no dense intermediate.
metal_feasible: YES — the strongest Apple Silicon precedent of all options: llama.cpp's Metal kernels already do this exact two-level scale decode on M-series GPUs. Porting the pattern into the fork's 1-bit qmm is a contained change.
est_savings: 6 + 16/8 = 8 bits/group: 0.125->0.0625 bpw; saves 0.0625 bpw = 210.9 MB = 5.56% of model bytes. New total 1.0625 bpw.
notes: CONSTRAINT-CROSSING: modifies scales, but gently — 6-bit linear sub-scale gives ~0.8% max error near the superblock max (worse for small scales in a superblock with outlier max). Likely the best accuracy-per-saved-byte of the 8-bit-class options and the least kernel risk. Composes orthogonally with block dropping/merging (metadata shrinks with whatever blocks survive).

method: SpQR-style bilevel int3 quantization of quantization statistics
source: SpQR, Dettmers et al. (arxiv.org/abs/2306.03078, ICLR 2024): 3-bit scales/zeros in second-level groups of 16 sharing f16 second-level scale+zero
mechanism: Asymmetric min-max quantize the f16 scales themselves to 3-bit integers; every 16 scale-codes share an f16 second-level scale and f16 zero-point. Our biases (zeros) could be handled identically per the SpQR recipe.
training_free: YES — min/max over existing statistics (SpQR's outlier/weight parts need calibration, but the bilevel-statistics component alone does not).
inference_native: YES with kernel work — SpQR ships fused GPU kernels consuming the bilevel format; nothing dense is materialized.
metal_feasible: PLAUSIBLE, more intricate than the 8-bit options: 3-bit unpack + two-level dequant in the 1-bit qmm kernel. Within 'modest kernel changes' but the fiddliest of the list.
est_savings: 3 + 32/16 = 5 bits/group: 0.125->0.0391 bpw; saves 0.0859 bpw = 290.0 MB = 7.64% of model bytes. New total 1.0391 bpw.
notes: CONSTRAINT-CROSSING with the largest value distortion of the practical options (8 levels per 16-scale window). SpQR validated this at 3-4-bit weights near-losslessly; at 1 bpw the scales carry ALL magnitude information, so damage must be measured within-format before trusting it. Best compression short of dictionary-4bit.

method: HQQ metadata quantization (deployed precedent: 8-bit scales g128, 8-bit zero-points)
source: HQQ, Badri & Shaji, Dropbox (dropbox.github.io/hqq_blog; github.com/dropbox/hqq quantize.py: quant_scale=8-bit group-128, quant_zero=8-bit)
mechanism: HQQ's meta-data option: quantize scales to int8 with group-size 128 over the scale tensor and zeros to int8 — i.e. shipping, calibration-free double quantization in a production library since 2023-2024. Only the metadata step applies to us; HQQ's weight solver must NOT be run (it would alter weights).
training_free: YES — explicitly calibration-free; closed-form rounding of existing metadata.
inference_native: YES in HQQ's own backends (torch/CUDA fused); for us same status as DQ: needs the MLX fork kernel to consume int8 scales + per-128 f16/f32 second-level constants.
metal_feasible: YES, modest — structurally identical kernel change to the QLoRA-DQ row.
est_savings: 8 + 16/128 = 8.125 bits/group: 0.125->0.0635 bpw; saves ~0.0615 bpw = ~207 MB = 5.5% of model bytes.
notes: CONSTRAINT-CROSSING (modifies scale/bias values). Value of this entry is precedent: proves 8-bit metadata over 1-bit-class weights is field-tested (HQQ supports 1-bit weight mode with quantized metadata). Their reported quality loss from metadata quantization at low bits was small but nonzero; they chose g128 over the scales specifically to bound it.

method: E8M0 power-of-two scales (OCP Microscaling / MXFP-style)
source: OCP MX spec via MXFP4 literature (emergentmind.com/topics/microscaling-fp4-quantization; NVFP4-vs-MXFP4 comparisons, spheron.network guide; MLX mxfp4/mxfp8 modes, ml-explore docs)
mechanism: Replace each f16 scale with an 8-bit pure exponent (power of two); dequant becomes an exponent add / bit-shift, no multiply.
training_free: YES — nearest-power-of-two rounding.
inference_native: YES — this is the one format mainline MLX already consumes natively (mxfp4/mxfp8 modes use e8m0 shared scales).
metal_feasible: YES, the most kernel-trivial of all: e8m0 decode already exists in upstream MLX Metal kernels; also note mx modes carry NO bias, so adapting to our affine (scale+bias) 1-bit groups still needs the fork.
est_savings: 0.125->0.0625 bpw; saves 0.0625 bpw = 210.9 MB = 5.56% of model bytes.
notes: CONSTRAINT-CROSSING and the WORST accuracy option: nearest-power-of-two rounding has up to ~33% relative scale error (literature consistently shows e8m0 losing to e4m3 scales; MR-GPTQ closes the gap only via rotations, which are weight-modifying and off-limits). For a 1-bit model where scale is the only magnitude signal, expect the largest within-format damage. Report for completeness; recommend against.

method: Shared/dictionary scales (per-tensor k-means codebook + 8-bit or 4-bit index; LUT kernel)
source: LUT/codebook kernel literature: SqueezeLLM (arxiv.org/abs/2306.07629, k-means codebooks, calibration-free variant); 'Highly Optimized Kernels and Fine-Grained Codebooks for LLM Inference' (arxiv.org/abs/2501.00032) for codebook-kernel viability
mechanism: Cluster each tensor's ~M group scales with k-means (k=256 or 16); store per-group index + tiny f16 codebook (512 B or 32 B per tensor). Kernel resolves scale via LUT held in threadgroup/constant memory — one extra indexed load.
training_free: YES — k-means over existing scale values only; selection/clustering, no data, no gradients.
inference_native: YES — codebook-lookup kernels count as native per the task rules, and LUT-in-shared-memory kernels are proven on GPUs and Arm; nothing dense is materialized.
metal_feasible: YES, trivial: a 256-entry half LUT fits easily in Metal threadgroup/constant memory; adding one lookup to the fork's 1-bit qmm is a small patch.
est_savings: k=256/8-bit index: saves 0.0625 bpw = 210.9 MB = 5.56% (new 1.0625 bpw). k=16/4-bit index: saves 0.0938 bpw = 316.4 MB = 8.33% of model bytes (new 1.0312 bpw) — the biggest saving on this list.
notes: Generally CONSTRAINT-CROSSING (snaps scales to centroids), BUT this is the one method with a potentially NON-crossing lossless special case: f16 scales have limited distinct bit patterns, and if a tensor's empirical distinct-scale count is <=256 (or <=65536 for a shared cross-tensor dictionary), the dictionary re-encoding is byte-exact value-preserving — pure storage relayout, fully inside rule 4. Cheap to check now from the existing census: count unique f16 scale values per tensor. At 4-bit/k=16 error grows; validate within-format.

method: NF-scale / quantile 8-bit coding of scales (NormalFloat-style code for the scale distribution)
source: Quantile quantization + NF4 machinery from QLoRA (arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314), applied to metadata; equivalent in kernel terms to the dictionary row
mechanism: Build a 256-entry code from the empirical quantiles (or fitted log-normal quantiles) of each tensor's scale distribution instead of linear int8 levels; store 8-bit code per group + 256-entry f16 decode table. Group scales are approximately log-normal, so quantile spacing beats linear int8/fp8 on SQNR at equal bits.
training_free: YES — quantiles of existing scales; no calibration data.
inference_native: YES — identical kernel to the dictionary/codebook row (256-entry LUT); NF4 decode-by-LUT is standard practice in bitsandbytes kernels.
metal_feasible: YES, trivial (same LUT patch as dictionary scales).
est_savings: 0.125->0.0625 bpw (+512 B/tensor table); saves 0.0625 bpw = 210.9 MB = 5.56% of model bytes.
notes: CONSTRAINT-CROSSING (re-rounds scales to quantile levels), but expected lowest distortion among the flat-8-bit family — strictly dominates linear int8 and usually fp8-e4m3 for log-normal scale distributions, at identical kernel cost. Practically it is the dictionary method with a smarter codebook; a k-means codebook (previous row) is MSE-optimal and should be preferred unless quantile construction is wanted for its distribution-free simplicity. Summary across all rows: hard ceiling 11.1% of bytes (421.9 MB) if scale metadata vanished entirely; realistic training-free range 5.5-8.3%; every option except the lossless-dictionary special case violates the weight-value-preservation rule and must be gated on within-format damage benchmarks (folded-vs-unfolded protocol), with the DSpark drafter already disabled per project rules.

method: Static vocabulary trimming (multilingual-to-target-language row deletion of embed + lm_head, tokenizer pruned to match)
source: Ushio et al., EMNLP 2023 Findings (arxiv.org/abs/2305.15020, aclanthology.org/2023.findings-emnlp.981); SqueezeBits blog (blog.squeezebits.com/vocabulary-trimming-methods); KaihuaTang/Qwen-Tokenizer-Pruner (github.com/KaihuaTang/Qwen-Tokenizer-Pruner); jordddan/Pruning-LLMs
mechanism: Rank the 248320 tokens by frequency on a target-language/domain corpus (or Unicode-script filter), keep top-k plus all special tokens and the 256 byte-level base tokens; delete the complementary rows from BOTH embedding and lm_head, prune the BPE merge rules whose products were deleted (maintaining merge closure), and remap token ids consistently across tokenizer/embed/lm_head. Qwen-Tokenizer-Pruner does exactly this for Qwen-family byte-level BPE (Bonsai's base is Qwen3.6-27B per docs/BONSAI_FACTS.md) and offers a 'lossless' mode with an old-vs-new tokenizer equivalence check on a support corpus.
training_free: YES — pure row selection/deletion; no gradients, no calibration-based weight updates. Corpus frequency counting is selection, not optimization of weight values.
inference_native: YES — surviving rows stay byte-identical 1-bit g128 (groups run along hidden dim: 5120/128 = 40 groups per row, so each vocab row is a self-contained run of u32 sign words + f16 scale/bias pairs; row deletion is pure slicing, no repacking). The trimmed matrices are consumed by the exact same quantized kernels.
metal_feasible: YES — vendored MLX fork has nn.QuantizedEmbedding (native quantized lookup) and quantized matmul with arbitrary row count; keep trimmed vocab a multiple of 128 for alignment safety. No kernel changes needed.
est_savings: Embed+lm_head = ~357 MB of the 4.21 GB language pack (untied, 2 x 179 MB at 1.125 bpw). Keep 80k rows: ~242 MB saved; keep 64k: ~265 MB; keep 32k: ~311 MB (~6-7% of pack). Plus proportional lm_head GEMV cut per decode token (small % of 27B decode; SqueezeBits' 1.585x decode speedup was on 1B tied-embedding models where embeddings dominate — expect low-single-digit % speedup here, memory is the real win).
notes: Measured quality: Ushio VT — trimming mT5/XLM-R to a 35% compression rate kept original QA/QG performance (39% NLI, 55% sentiment), sometimes exceeding the untrimmed model. SqueezeBits — up to ~40% frequency-based trim with stable English/Korean benchmark scores. Tokenizer interaction (the crux): INPUT side crashes only if the tokenizer can still emit a deleted id, so either prune merges coherently (byte-level BPE falls back to shorter subtokens; all text stays encodable because the 256 byte tokens are the alphabet floor) or use lossless mode guaranteeing identical tokenization on the support corpus. OUTPUT side never crashes — deleted rows are simply ungenerable and the softmax silently renormalizes. Never delete: chat-template/thinking-tag specials (Bonsai convention item 7) or byte tokens (needed to emit arbitrary unicode). Caveat for our harness: off-policy KL vs the unfolded baseline needs an id-permutation map to align logits; commit the remap table with the pack. Best fit of all surveyed methods with bonsai-fold constraints; orthogonal to block dropping (composes additively with H4 merges).

method: Output-side-only lm_head row trimming (frequency-ranked static subset; input embeddings and tokenizer untouched)
source: FR-Spec, ACL 2025 (arxiv.org/abs/2502.14856, github.com/thunlp/FR-Spec); VocabTrim (arxiv.org/abs/2506.22694); classic NMT vocabulary selection (L'Hostis et al. 2016)
mechanism: Delete only lm_head rows for tokens outside a frequency-ranked subset (FR-Spec uses top-32k of a 128k+ vocab); the full tokenizer and full input embedding matrix are kept, so every input encodes exactly as before and the model retains full multilingual understanding — only its GENERATION vocabulary shrinks. FR-Spec/VocabTrim apply this to speculative-decoding drafters; the same row selection applies directly to the target model's lm_head.
training_free: YES — frequency-ranked row selection, no weight modification (both papers are explicitly retraining-free).
inference_native: YES — same row-slicing argument as full trimming; surviving lm_head rows byte-identical 1-bit g128.
metal_feasible: YES — smaller quantized GEMV with existing kernels; nothing new needed.
est_savings: lm_head only: 179 MB total; keep 64k rows saves ~133 MB, keep 32k saves ~156 MB. Logit GEMV compute per decode token cut 74-87% (FR-Spec reports 75% LM-head compute reduction at top-32k).
notes: Safest first step and the cleanest answer to the input-vs-output asymmetry: zero tokenizer risk, zero input-side unseen-token handling, no id remapping on the input path (keep original ids, only compact the lm_head with an output-id map). IMPORTANT distribution caveat: FR-Spec preserves the exact output distribution only because the full target model verifies drafts — that exactness does NOT transfer to us since bonsai-fold disables speculative decoding on folded models (DSpark drafter constraint); a standalone trimmed lm_head renormalizes probability over surviving rows, so it is lossy-but-tiny for frequency-selected subsets (long-tail token mass). Evidence the tail is negligible: FR-Spec's premise that vocabulary usage is heavily long-tailed; VocabTrim shows drafter acceptance rates largely preserved after trimming. Deleted-token effect at output: those tokens can never be sampled — verify thinking-tag and template specials retained. Damage should be gated with the project's within-format KL harness against the 4-bit-KV noise floor (0.0009/0.0023 nats, Table 6).

method: Dynamic vocabulary-restricted decoding (VocabTailor-style hybrid: per-input dynamic + task-static lm_head subset, computed via gathered quantized matmul)
mechanism: Keep tokenizer and embedding intact (embedding lookup is cheap/sparse; VocabTailor offloads it to CPU); at runtime compute logits only over a union of (a) token ids present in the current input/prompt and (b) an offline-profiled task-specific static set — exploiting 'lexical locality'. No weights are modified or deleted from disk; the restriction is applied at the matmul.
training_free: YES — only offline dataset profiling to build the static set; no weight changes at all.
inference_native: YES — implementable as a row-gather over the untouched 1-bit lm_head; the vendored MLX fork already ships gather_qmm (vendor/mlx/benchmarks/python/gather_qmm_bench.py), so gathered quantized matmul over selected rows is an existing Metal kernel, not new backend work.
metal_feasible: YES — gather_qmm exists in the fork; modest glue code only. On the 64 GB M4 Max, CPU-offload of embeddings is unnecessary — the win here is compute, not memory.
est_savings: 0 bytes on disk (weights untouched — strongest possible weight-value preservation); up to ~90% of lm_head GEMV FLOPs per decode token at ~10% effective vocab. Peak-memory savings only matter on smaller devices.
notes: Measured (Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen-1.7B class): code completion 53.87% Pass@1 at 11.2% vocab (naive static-only pruning collapses to 8.1%); information extraction F1 62.7 at 0.08% vocab vs 38.4 full (restriction acted as beneficial constraint); MT EN-ZH improved at 12.5% vocab; summarization/math undegraded at 16-55% retention; tolerance threshold tau=0.01 bounds worst-case loss. Input/output asymmetry is the paper's core insight: input side must stay full (tokenizer + embeddings) because unseen input tokens are common; output side tolerates aggressive restriction because generation draws from a small locality. Task-conditional, not general chat — fits benchmark-style evals better than open-ended use. Also renormalizes the output distribution (same caveat as static output trimming).

method: Embedding matrix sharing / post-hoc weight tying (replace lm_head with embedding rows or vice versa to store one matrix instead of two)
source: Press & Wolf 2017 (Using the Output Embedding to Improve LMs); 'Weight Tying Biases Token Embeddings Towards the Output Space' (arxiv.org/abs/2603.26663)
mechanism: Tied models store one matrix used for both input lookup and output projection. Bonsai is UNTIED (docs/BONSAI_FACTS.md: embeddings/LM head ~2.5B = two separate 1.27B matrices), so the only training-free move is post-hoc substitution of one matrix for the other.
training_free: YES in mechanics (copy/substitute), but see notes — it is effectively a wholesale value replacement of one matrix.
inference_native: YES trivially (same format, one matrix).
metal_feasible: YES trivially.
est_savings: Would save ~179 MB (one full matrix) — but unusable.
notes: RULED OUT on measured evidence, report as negative result. The 2026 tying-bias study shows untied models learn near-orthogonal input vs output spaces (tied matrices align with untied OUTPUT matrices at mean cosine 0.719, but untied input vs output matrices show limited similarity even after fitting a linear map) — substituting one for the other in an untied model destroys either input encoding or next-token prediction. Also constraint-crossing in spirit: the substituted role receives entirely wrong 'values'. FLAGGED: value-modifying-equivalent and quality-catastrophic; do not spend GPU time on it beyond, at most, one cheap KL sanity probe if a table row is wanted.

method: Low-rank / tensor-train embedding factorization (TensorGPT TT-decomposition; ALBERT-style SVD factorization of embed/lm_head)
source: TensorGPT (arxiv.org/abs/2307.00526); ALBERT (Lan et al. 2020) for the SVD-factorization pattern
mechanism: Replace the [vocab x hidden] matrix with low-rank or Matrix-Product-State factors reconstructed at lookup time. TensorGPT converts each token embedding to an MPS via closed-form tensor-train decomposition (no gradient training).
training_free: TensorGPT: YES (closed-form TTD, no fine-tuning). SVD variants: YES in closed form, though most published pipelines add recovery fine-tuning.
inference_native: NO for bonsai-fold — factors must be computed on DEQUANTIZED f16 embeddings, so the stored form is FP factor cores, not the 1-bit g128 format the kernels consume; re-quantizing factors to 1-bit is a second lossy value modification with no published evidence at this scale. Input-side lookup (reconstruct one row per token) could be made cheap, but the lm_head side needs either dense reconstruction per step (a decompress-to-dense step, explicitly disallowed) or new factored-projection Metal kernels (beyond 'modest kernel changes').
metal_feasible: NOT without new kernels for MPS-form projection; no existing MLX/Metal support.
est_savings: Reference only: 39-66x embedding-layer compression on GPT-2/CerebrasGPT scale with comparable task performance at ~2-3x compression (some settings beat baseline). Numbers are from FP models under ~1B params; unvalidated at 27B/1-bit.
notes: FLAGGED: constraint-crossing on (2) inference-native and (4) value preservation — every reconstructed embedding is an approximation of the original values, and interaction between TT approximation error and 1-bit quantization error is uncharacterized. Report for completeness; do not implement.

method: Hash / compositional / Kronecker embeddings (shared-parameter embedding tables)
source: Svenstrup et al. 2017 (Hash Embeddings, NeurIPS); Kronecker byte-level embeddings (arxiv.org/abs/2605.29459)
mechanism: Represent each token as a learned combination of a small shared pool of component vectors selected by hash functions (or Kronecker-structured byte-level factors), so the table size is decoupled from vocab size.
training_free: NO — the component vectors and importance weights must be learned; there is no closed-form conversion from an existing dense (let alone 1-bit) embedding matrix.
inference_native: N/A (fails constraint 1 first); would also need custom lookup kernels.
metal_feasible: N/A.
est_savings: N/A (order-of-magnitude table reductions in from-scratch training regimes only).
notes: EXCLUDED outright by the training-free hard constraint. Listed so the survey is complete and nobody re-litigates it later.

method: Practical playbook for row deletion vs the Bonsai tokenizer (cross-cutting engineering notes for whichever trim variant is chosen)
source: Synthesis of the above + repo facts (docs/BONSAI_FACTS.md; vendor/mlx); Qwen-Tokenizer-Pruner for the Qwen-specific procedure
mechanism: Bonsai inherits Qwen3.6's byte-level BPE. Input-side safety invariant: an embedding row may be deleted only if the (possibly pruned) tokenizer can never emit its id — guaranteed by keeping the 256 byte-alphabet tokens plus maintaining merge closure (delete every merge producing a deleted token and every merge downstream of it); text containing trimmed tokens then encodes as more, shorter tokens (mild, familiar-to-model segmentation shift; Qwen-Tokenizer-Pruner's lossless mode verifies encode-equivalence on a support corpus). Output-side invariant: lm_head row deletion is always crash-safe; it silently renormalizes the softmax and makes deleted tokens ungenerable — so byte tokens and all chat-template/thinking-tag specials must survive or the model loses the ability to emit arbitrary unicode / follow the template. Update SPECIAL_START_ID-style config offsets after remapping (Qwen-pruner gotcha).
training_free: YES (procedure, not a method).
inference_native: YES — g128 groups lie along hidden dim (40 groups per 5120-wide row), so vocab-dim row slicing never splits a quantization group; surviving rows are byte-identical. Keep the trimmed vocab a multiple of 128 for kernel alignment comfort.
metal_feasible: YES — nn.QuantizedEmbedding + standard/gathered quantized matmul all present in the vendored MLX fork.
est_savings: See per-method rows; combined ceiling ~311 MB (~7% of 4.21 GB pack) at 32k retained vocab, both matrices.
notes: Evaluation-harness caveats specific to bonsai-fold: (1) within-format KL comparisons vs the unfolded 1-bit baseline require an id-alignment map after any remap (compare in original-id space); (2) on-policy generation evals must confirm thinking-mode tags still open/close (sampling: temp 0.7, top-p 0.95, top-k 20, thinking on); (3) speculative decoding is already disabled on folded models, so no drafter/vocab interaction to manage; (4) vocab trimming composes with block dropping/merging — memory savings are additive and independent, matching pending task #10 (orthogonal-axis compression, width/vocab censuses); (5) recommended damage gate: forward-KL vs unfolded on the standard corpora, judged against the 4-bit-KV noise floor (0.0009 on-policy / 0.0023 off-policy nats).

method: MLX native sparse matmul kernels (N:M, CSR, general) — status check
mechanism: N/A — none exist. Issue #2728 '[Feature] Kernels for sparse matmuls' was marked won't-fix by maintainer zcbenz (Mar 2026) citing JAX's abandoned jax.experimental.sparse as precedent ('no active development on sparse matrix in other frameworks'), closed May 2026. PR #2796 implemented sparse_matmul_csr with a working Metal backend (tested M2 Pro) but was closed unmerged — maintainer: 'proper support for sparse APIs would require considerable refactoring.' No N:M kernels exist or are planned anywhere in MLX.
training_free: n/a
inference_native: n/a
metal_feasible: Upstream MLX: no, and explicitly won't-fix as of Mar 2026. The rejected #2796 CSR Metal kernel code exists and could be salvaged into our patched fork, but it targets f32/f16 dense values, not the packed 1-bit format.
est_savings: none available off the shelf
notes: Definitive answer to the headline question: upstream MLX has no sparse matmul story and has formally declined one. Anything sparse on our stack must come from our own fork patches.

method: mx.block_masked_mm (MLX built-in block-masked matmul)
mechanism: Matmul where 32x32 or 64x64 blocks are masked out and skipped. This is MLX's only shipping block-sparse compute primitive.
training_free: yes (a mask is pure selection)
inference_native: NO for our model — it consumes dense f16/f32 operands only. There is no quantized variant: it cannot read the u32-packed 1-bit + g128 scale/bias format, so using it would require dequantize-to-dense (violates constraint 2). Also mask-style: masked blocks are still stored, so zero memory savings.
metal_feasible: yes, it ships in MLX Metal today — but only for dense tensors
est_savings: 0 bytes; compute-only, and unusable on quantized weights without a new masked-qmm kernel
notes: Confirms MLX/Metal can do block-skip matmul in principle. A 'block_masked_qmm' marrying this with quantized.h's QuantizedBlockLoader does not exist and would be our kernel work (see g128 group-sparsity finding).

method: gather_mm / gather_qmm (MLX quantized gather matmul, ex block_sparse_qmm)
mechanism: Index-gathered quantized matmul built for MoE routing: selects whole weight matrices/slices by index and runs the fused 1-bit-capable quantized kernel on them. Despite the original 'block_sparse_qmm' name, it is matrix-granularity selection, not intra-matrix sparsity.
training_free: yes (index selection)
inference_native: yes — operates directly on the packed quantized format
metal_feasible: yes, shipping in MLX Metal today, including for quantized weights
est_savings: none for weight compression per se; relevant only if we ever express folded blocks as a gathered subset of stored blocks
notes: The only 'sparse-named' kernel family in MLX that actually composes with our 1-bit format. Granularity is far too coarse for weight sparsity, but it is the existence proof that selection-style kernels over the quantized format are native on this stack.

method: mlx-sparse (third-party COO/CSR/CSC package for MLX)
source: https://github.com/waleed-sh/mlx-sparse (announced in mlx#2728/#148 threads, May 2026); https://mlx-sparse.readthedocs.io
mechanism: MLX-native sparse array containers with sparse-dense and sparse-sparse ops; C++ CPU/Accelerate backends, Metal kernels only 'when and where available'. Early beta, single-author, APIs unstable, no CUDA.
training_free: yes (it's a linear-algebra package)
inference_native: no for us — stores f32/f16 values; no composition with MLX's quantized format, no N:M, not built for LLM decode paths
metal_feasible: partially (some Metal kernels), but not production-grade and not quantization-aware
est_savings: n/a
notes: The only living sparse-MLX code as of mid-2026. Useful as reference Metal sparse-kernel code if we build our own, not as a deployment path for a 27B 1-bit decoder.

method: Sparse-BitNet (MSR, Mar 2026) — joint 1.58-bit + N:M sparsity
mechanism: Trains BitNet with dynamic 6:8 (primary) or 2:4 N:M masks recomputed every step from FP master weights ('we train Sparse-BitNet from scratch, optimizing the master weights end-to-end'). Key result: 1.58-bit models tolerate N:M far better than FP (2:4: +5.7% normalized PPL vs +18.8% for BF16). Speedup <=1.30x via an in-house 6:8 sparse operator on NVIDIA A100/B200.
training_free: NO — requires sparse pretraining or dense-to-sparse schedules; the paper shows late/post-hoc sparsification degrades badly and offers no post-training recipe. Hard fail on constraint 1.
inference_native: yes on their stack (custom sparse operator), but that stack is CUDA
metal_feasible: no — kernels are NVIDIA-only; Apple M4 GPUs have no sparse tensor units and Metal/MPS exposes no N:M path
est_savings: <=1.30x speedup on NVIDIA; memory saving ~0 at these bit-widths (see next finding)
notes: No successors/follow-ups found yet (paper is ~5 months old, models 0.5B-3B). The transferable nugget for us is the accuracy claim only: extreme-low-bit weights are unusually robust to structured masking — mild supporting evidence for our deletion-based program, not a deployable method.

method: N:M semi-structured sparsity applied to 1-bit weights (any variant) — arithmetic dead-end
source: own analysis from the pack format (u32 sign bits + f16 scale/bias per g128, ~1.125 bpw)
mechanism: Storage accounting: dense 1-bit costs 4 bits per 4 weights. 2:4 sparse costs 2 sign bits + position metadata: 4 bits with NVIDIA-style 2-bit-per-survivor encoding (6 total), or log2(C(4,2))=2.58 bits at the information-theoretic optimum (4.58 total). Either way >= 4 bits dense. 6:8: 6 sign bits + log2(C(8,6))=4.8 bits = 10.8 vs 8 dense. At ~1 bpw the mask metadata costs more than the weights it removes.
training_free: yes (magnitude/Wanda-style mask selection would be training-free)
inference_native: no encoding exists that is both smaller than dense and consumable by any Apple Silicon kernel
metal_feasible: no — and even with kernels it would be pointless: memory savings are NEGATIVE, and the remaining upside (compute skip) is worthless because M4 Max decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and Apple GPUs have no sparse tensor units
est_savings: negative memory delta (~+15-50% on the sign payload depending on encoding); ~0 latency
notes: This is the decisive argument, independent of the kernel gap: semi-structured sparsity is self-defeating at 1 bpw. Sparsity only pays on this format at granularities where deleted units carry their own scale/bias metadata — i.e., whole g128 groups, rows, or larger (next two findings).

method: 128-aligned structured width pruning (MLP-neuron / head / vocab-row deletion, Wanda/FLAP-style scoring)
source: Wanda arXiv:2306.11695 (https://github.com/locuslab/wanda); FLAP arXiv:2312.11983; alignment analysis: own, from pack format
mechanism: Delete entire MLP intermediate channels in 128-aligned blocks: drops whole rows of gate/up_proj (each row's packed u32 words + g128 scales are self-contained) and the matching 128-aligned K-groups of down_proj (group-aligned, so packed words + their f16 scale/bias delete cleanly). Head_dim-aligned attention-head deletion and vocab-row deletion of the 1-bit embedding/lm_head (248320 rows) work the same way. Result is simply SMALLER DENSE 1-bit matrices in the exact same format — surviving bytes byte-identical. Rank channels with weight-only stats (group-scale magnitudes) or Wanda-style activation norms from forward passes.
training_free: yes — pure deletion/selection; calibration (if used) only ranks what to delete, never updates weights. Fully weight-value-preserving.
inference_native: yes — stock mx.quantized_matmul consumes the smaller matrices; nothing to decompress, no mask, no metadata
metal_feasible: YES, today, with ZERO kernel changes — the only sparsity-adjacent form with this property on our stack
est_savings: MLP is ~3*5120*17408*64 ≈ 17.1B of ~27B params (~63% of the ~3.8 GB pack). Pruning 12.5-25% of intermediate channels (17408 -> 15232/13056) saves ~8-16% of total bytes with proportional decode-bandwidth speedup; embeddings+lm_head are another ~9.4% of bytes, so task-dependent vocab pruning of 50% adds ~4.7%. Within-format damage unknown — must be measured against the unfolded 1-bit baseline.
notes: VERDICT CANDIDATE #1. Orthogonal to and stackable with block dropping/merging. Only constraint nuance: Wanda-style activation scoring uses calibration forward passes — selection only, arguably compliant, but flag the choice in the lab notebook; the pure weight-only variant (rank by g128 scale magnitude) avoids the question entirely.

method: Intra-matrix g128 group sparsity via custom masked/compacted qmv-qmm (novel; no prior art found)
source: own design; kernel substrate: mlx/backend/metal/kernels/quantized.h (QuantizedBlockLoader, qmv/qvm/qmm variants — see deepwiki.com/ml-explore/mlx/7.2), our patched MLX fork
mechanism: Delete whole quantization groups (128 sign bits + f16 scale + f16 bias ≈ 160 bits each) anywhere in a matrix; store surviving groups compacted with a per-row group-index list (or 1 bit/group bitmap ≈ 0.8% overhead). Kernel change: the K-loop iterates the survivor list instead of a dense range — structurally similar to what QVM/QMM split-K loops already do. Deletion-only, survivors byte-identical.
training_free: yes — group selection by scale magnitude and/or calibration activation norms (selection only)
inference_native: yes IF we write the kernel — the compacted form is what the kernel consumes directly; no dense reconstruction
metal_feasible: plausibly, as a 'modest kernel change' to our fork (new loop bound + indirection in qmv/qmm); but it is genuinely novel — no implementation exists in MLX, llama.cpp, MPS, or any paper we found, so we'd be writing and validating it ourselves
est_savings: ≈ group-sparsity fraction of the affected layers' bytes (metadata ~1%); 25% group sparsity in MLP ≈ 16% of model bytes, plus bandwidth-proportional decode speedup since decode is memory-bound
notes: VERDICT CANDIDATE #2 — the finer-grained sibling of width pruning, needing real kernel work. Recommend only if 128-aligned width pruning saturates first. Accuracy risk: a deleted group zeroes 128 contiguous input contributions including the affine bias term; damage profile unstudied anywhere.

method: TEAL / CATS / SparseInfer — training-free activation sparsity
source: TEAL arXiv:2408.14690 (ICLR 2025), https://github.com/fasterdecoding/teal; CATS arXiv:2404.08763; SparseInfer arXiv:2411.12692; PowerInfer SOSP'24
mechanism: Threshold hidden-state magnitudes at runtime (TEAL: 40-50% model-wide sparsity, thresholds set from calibration histograms), then use sparse GEMV kernels that skip weight loads for zeroed channels; 1.53-1.8x decode speedups with Triton/CUDA kernels. Weights completely untouched.
training_free: yes (TEAL/CATS; PowerInfer and LLM-in-a-flash style predictor approaches are NOT — trained predictors, ReLU-family models — excluded)
inference_native: weights stay in native packed form, but the speedup requires sparse-gather GEMV kernels that do not exist for Metal/MLX — no port found anywhere (llama.cpp Metal computes FFNs dense; SparseInfer/PowerInfer are CUDA/CPU)
metal_feasible: would require custom fork kernels; worse, our u32-packed K-dim means skip granularity is 32-128 weights, so realizable sparsity (and speedup) drops well below TEAL's per-element numbers
est_savings: 0 bytes — model size unchanged; hypothetical 1.2-1.5x decode latency if a group-granular Metal kernel were built
notes: Compliant with every constraint on paper (weights byte-identical) but delivers no compression, which is bonsai-fold's actual objective. Report as latency-only, low-priority; the same kernel investment spent on finding #8 buys memory AND latency.

method: SparseGPT / one-shot 2:4 pruning pipelines (prune-then-quantize stacks, Sparse-Marlin deployment)
source: SparseGPT arXiv:2301.00774; vLLM llm-compressor 2:4+W4A16 example (docs.vllm.ai/projects/llm-compressor); Sparse-Marlin kernels (CUDA)
mechanism: One-shot layer-wise sparse regression: prunes to 2:4 and RECONSTRUCTS surviving weights using second-order calibration statistics; standard stacks prune the FP model first, quantize second; deployment kernels (Sparse-Marlin, cuSPARSELt) are NVIDIA sparse-tensor-core only.
training_free: nominally (no gradient steps), but SparseGPT's weight reconstruction is calibration-based weight optimization — FLAGGED constraint-crossing on both constraint 1 and the weight-preservation rule. Wanda-selection-only variants avoid this but then collapse into finding #6's metadata dead-end.
inference_native: only on NVIDIA sparse tensor cores
metal_feasible: no — no Metal kernels exist, no Apple hardware support, and we start from an already-1-bit model (the pipelines assume FP input; we have no FP weights and FP baselines are out of scope anyway)
est_savings: ~50% weight-count on FP models in their setting; not transferable to our stack
notes: Reportable lineage only. Every practical semi-structured deployment path in 2025-2026 (llm-compressor, Sparse-Marlin, NVIDIA ASP) terminates in Ampere+ sparse tensor cores; none has an Apple analogue.

method: Core ML / ANE sparse weight compression (apple coremltools opt-pruning) — Apple's only shipping sparse path
mechanism: Magnitude pruning + sparse weight storage in the Core ML model format; the ANE runtime decodes sparse weights with real latency/size benefits on recent chips. Composable with palettization/quantization inside Core ML's own format.
training_free: yes (post-training magnitude pruning variant exists)
inference_native: yes, within Core ML/ANE
metal_feasible: NO for us — this is a different backend (Core ML compiler + ANE runtime), not our patched MLX/Metal fork; adopting it means porting Bonsai's 1-bit g128-affine format into Core ML, i.e., exactly the 'whole new backend' constraint 3 prohibits
est_savings: n/a on our stack
notes: Included to answer 'any Metal sparse-inference work?' precisely: Apple's sparsity investment went into Core ML/ANE, not Metal compute or MLX. Nothing to salvage for bonsai-fold.

method: VERDICT — deployable sparsity on the MLX/Metal 1-bit stack
mechanism: Three-part answer. (a) Kernels: MLX has no N:M/CSR/general sparse matmul and has formally won't-fixed the request (mlx#2728, Mar 2026); its only sparse-ish primitives are block_masked_mm (dense-only) and gather_qmm (matrix-granularity MoE selection). Apple's Metal/MPS exposes no sparse matmul and M4 GPUs have no sparse tensor hardware; Apple's sparsity work lives in Core ML/ANE, a different backend. (b) Semi-structured: N:M on ~1 bpw weights is arithmetically self-defeating — position metadata (2.6-4 bits per 4 weights) costs as much as or more than the 1-bit weights it removes, so even perfect kernels would yield negative memory savings on a bandwidth-bound decoder. Sparse-BitNet, the one paper marrying 1-bit and N:M, requires sparse pretraining and NVIDIA kernels. (c) Activation sparsity (TEAL) is training-free and weight-preserving but saves zero bytes and has no Metal port.
training_free: see per-method rows
inference_native: see per-method rows
metal_feasible: exactly one form is deployable WITHOUT kernel work: 128-aligned structured deletion (MLP-intermediate channels, attention heads, vocab rows) — it degenerates to smaller dense matrices in the unchanged 1-bit format, consumed by stock quantized_matmul, surviving weights byte-identical. One more form (g128 group sparsity with a compacted-loop qmv/qmm) is feasible as a modest patch to our fork but is novel engineering with no prior art.
est_savings: realistic near-term: ~8-16% of pack bytes from 12.5-25% aligned MLP-width pruning (+~5% optional vocab pruning), stackable with block dropping/merging; damage to be measured within-format per project rules
notes: Recommendation: pursue 128-aligned width pruning as the sparsity arm (fits every hard constraint, zero kernel risk, complements depth compression); hold g128 group sparsity in reserve; drop N:M, activation sparsity, and all CUDA-lineage pipelines from consideration. Sources: github.com/ml-explore/mlx issues/2728, pull/2796, pull/1124, pull/2040; ml-explore.github.io block_masked_mm docs; arXiv 2603.05168, 2408.14690, 2411.12692, 2306.11695, 2301.00774; github.com/waleed-sh/mlx-sparse; github.com/apple/coremltools; github.com/fasterdecoding/teal; github.com/locuslab/wanda.

method: Wanda-sp (structured Wanda, per-channel/head aggregation)
source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.11695 (Wanda); structured adaptation defined in FLAP paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.11983
mechanism: Saliency = sum over the channel/head of |W_ij|*||X_j||_2 from a small calibration forward pass; delete lowest-scoring MLP channels / attention heads outright. Pure selection, zero weight updates.
training_free: YES - calibration forward passes only, no gradients, no updates
inference_native: YES - result is just a smaller standard model; MLX quantized kernels consume it unchanged
metal_feasible: YES - output-row deletion is trivial in the g128 packed format (drop packed row + its scale/bias groups); input-dim deletion must be 128-group aligned (see gap-analysis row)
est_savings: 10-20% of block params (~0.35-0.7 GB of the ~3.8 GB pack) before steep FP-model damage; headroom on an already-1-bit model unknown - measure within-format per project rules
notes: The baseline width criterion; FLAP's own comparisons show it is the weakest of the family. Compute saliency on dequantized effective weights (sign*scale+bias per g128 group), not raw sign bits.

method: FLAP (Fluctuation-based Adaptive Structured Pruning), AAAI 2024
mechanism: Fluctuation metric: sample variance of each input feature weighted by squared column norm - low-variance channels have outputs recoverable by a constant. Adaptive global structure search sets per-layer/per-module ratios. Then optional bias compensation adds mean-activation*pruned-weights as a bias term.
training_free: YES - 3-5 min on one GPU, no retraining
inference_native: YES
metal_feasible: YES - selection+deletion identical mechanics to Wanda-sp; bias compensation only needs a bias vector on linear layers (MLX supports bias)
est_savings: 10-30% structured ratios on LLaMA with best retraining-free quality of its generation; clearly beats LLM-Pruner and Wanda-sp without any recovery
notes: PARTIAL FLAG: bias compensation is a calibration-derived NEW parameter - surviving weights stay byte-identical, but it adds values the original model never had. Decision needed: run selection-only (pure), or accept the added-bias variant as a flagged arm. The adaptive ratio-allocation piece is criterion-agnostic and reusable.

method: MultiPruner (Intel Labs, extends BlockPruner)
mechanism: Iterative multidimensional training-free pruning: first residual blocks (depth), then MLP channels, then attention heads, under one global budget; candidates ranked by calibration perplexity/loss. Pure deletion, no reconstruction.
training_free: YES
inference_native: YES
metal_feasible: YES - directly composable with bonsai-fold's existing block-drop machinery; head removal must keep GQA q:kv ratio integral; channel removal 128-aligned
est_savings: Reported to beat prior training-free methods at ~22% compression with better zero-shot accuracy
notes: Closest published analog to bonsai-fold's trajectory (depth axis exhausted, width added on top). Its iterative search means many candidate evaluations - chunk under the 2h job limit; our existing KL-vs-parent harness is the natural inner metric.

method: DIET (dimension-wise global pruning via task-importance voting)
mechanism: Profile activation magnitudes on ~100 samples per task across several tasks; majority-vote the per-task importance rankings into one global dimension mask. Pure mask/selection.
training_free: YES - explicitly no training or heavy precompute
inference_native: YES
metal_feasible: YES - same deletion mechanics
est_savings: At 20% structured sparsity on Gemma-2 2B, ~10% average accuracy over prior structured SOTA; persists across scales
notes: Cheap orthogonal upgrade: multi-domain calibration voting counters single-calibration-set bias (a documented failure mode). Applicable to whichever saliency criterion we adopt - vote across our existing eval domains.

method: CoCurve (cross-module co-pruning curvature)
mechanism: Second-order Taylor of token-level KL between frozen model and masked copy gives a Fisher matrix; off-diagonals capture co-pruning interactions (two individually weak units jointly indispensable). Full MxM interaction recovered from M forward passes, no gradients; one budgeted quadratic program selects the joint set of heads + FFN channel groups. No weight changes, no recovery.
training_free: YES - calibration-only, fine-tuning-free, gradient-free
inference_native: YES
metal_feasible: YES - forward passes run in stock MLX; the QP is CPU-side scipy
est_savings: Abstract gives no headline ratio; claims consistent gains over independent ranking at equal budgets
notes: Philosophically matches bonsai-fold's Phase-1 finding that deletion interactions are non-additive (k-set results). The masked-forward Fisher estimation is nearly identical in cost shape to our off-policy KL singles chain - strongest candidate for the selection engine.

method: Gate-Norm (data-free attention-sublayer pruning)
mechanism: Weight-only criterion ranking attention sublayers by query-key coupling norm; delete the least-coupled whole attention sublayers (MLP stays). No calibration data, no forward passes, no weight modification, no special kernels.
training_free: YES - fully data-free, runs in under a second
inference_native: YES - deleting an attn sublayer is a config + surgery change, like our block drops but finer
metal_feasible: YES - trivially
est_savings: 8-16 of 40 attn sublayers removed on LLaMA-13B within ~2% zero-shot, 1.30x throughput. On Bonsai attention is a modest byte fraction, so mostly a latency win plus a few % params
notes: Adds a third granularity between whole-block drop and head pruning: attn-only removal. Verify the coupling criterion on dequantized 1-bit weights (sign*scale+bias) - untested on extreme quantization. DSpark speculative-decoding disable rule already covers the layer-index hazard.

method: CAP (Causal Attribution Pruning of attention heads)
mechanism: For each head, estimate expected degradation when the head is masked during forward passes on a small reasoning calibration set; causal head-level scores guide pruning. Forward-only, no gradients, no weight updates (head-scoring stage is usable standalone for pure head deletion).
training_free: YES
inference_native: YES for whole-head deletion
metal_feasible: YES - masked-forward scoring is exactly our off-policy ablation pattern
est_savings: Claims reasoning preservation at matched ratios (abstract gives no hard numbers)
notes: Reasoning-preservation focus fits thinking-mode Bonsai (temp 0.7 / thinking on). Its weight-level second stage is finer than we need; use the head-attribution stage only.

method: COMPACT (vocab pruning + FFN channel pruning)
mechanism: Prunes rare vocabulary rows from embedding + lm_head, and FFN intermediate channels scored by common-token-weighted activations; keeps a standard transformer, runnable in stock engines. Selection/deletion only.
training_free: YES
inference_native: YES - explicitly designed for standard-architecture output (their critique of SliceGPT)
metal_feasible: YES - embedding/lm_head rows are independent in the g128 packed format, so vocab-row deletion is byte-exact; needs a tokenizer-id remap table at load
est_savings: Bonsai embed+head = 2 x 248320 x 5120 = 2.54B params = ~0.36 GB at 1.125 bpw (~9% of pack). Halving the unusually large 248K vocab saves ~0.18 GB plus a ~2x lm_head matmul speedup per token
notes: Directly aligned with the pending 'width/vocab censuses' task. Risk: multilingual/rare-token capability loss is invisible to English perplexity - pick within-format eval sets carefully.

method: RAP (RoPE-Aligned KV-channel pruning)
mechanism: Delete least-useful Wk/Wv output channels in RoPE-aligned pairs (whole rotation pairs) to shrink KV head_dim, keeping positional semantics intact. Deletion-based; abstract mentions no fine-tuning.
training_free: YES (apparent; verify in full text)
inference_native: PARTIAL - attention must run with reduced KV dim and a RoPE frequency-index map; not stock MLX attention
metal_feasible: PARTIAL - Wk/Wv row deletion is format-native, but the RoPE index map + reduced head_dim needs a modest patch in our MLX fork
est_savings: 30% KV-cache reduction with preserved accuracy on 3B-14B Llama/Mistral/Qwen; weight savings minor
notes: Wins KV memory (long-context headroom on the 64GB box), not pack size. Composes with quantization per the paper. Verify Bonsai uses standard RoPE and check q/k head_dim before scoping.

method: SliceGPT (rotation + slicing) - REJECTED
mechanism: Folds PCA orthogonal rotations into every weight matrix, then slices rows/columns of the rotated weights.
training_free: YES nominally, but it rewrites every surviving weight value
inference_native: NO for us - rotated weights are dense FP and cannot be re-expressed in the frozen 1-bit sign+scale+bias format without requantizing (a weight update); also breaks HF/vLLM compat per COMPACT
metal_feasible: N/A
est_savings: 20-30% on FP models (reference only)
notes: CONSTRAINT-CROSSING, unrescuable: violates byte-identical surviving weights by construction. The whole rotation family (QuaRot-style descendants) is excluded for the same reason.

method: Reconstruction family: STAT / CORP / Olica / LIAR / OSSCAR - FLAGGED
mechanism: Delete heads/channels, then closed-form update the remaining weights (ridge regression, matrix factorization, layer-wise reconstruction) so retained units absorb the removed units' function.
training_free: Nominally yes (no gradient descent), but all perform calibration-based weight UPDATES - rejected under our definition
inference_native: Updated weights are FP and would need requantization to 1-bit - a second violation
metal_feasible: N/A as-is
est_savings: Typically 1-3 ppl points better than pure selection at 20-30% ratios (FP models)
notes: CONSTRAINT-CROSSING (calibration-based weight optimization). Reportable value: their selection-vs-reconstruction ablations quantify exactly what pure selection gives up; some saliency halves are reusable standalone.

method: SlimLLM - FLAGGED (borderline)
mechanism: Holistic whole-channel/whole-head importance (not summed element scores) + layer-wise adaptive ratios + linear-regression recovery of the output matrix.
training_free: Selection stage yes; recovery stage is a calibration-based weight update
inference_native: YES if recovery is skipped
metal_feasible: YES for the selection stage
est_savings: SOTA claims on LLaMA at unspecified ratios (with recovery)
notes: FLAG the regression-recovery step; the holistic head/channel importance metric itself is selection-only and directly reusable as an alternative criterion to FLAP's.

method: Numerical Pruning (AAAI 2025) - FLAGGED
mechanism: Training-free Newton-method numerical scores for Attention/MLP structures, plus a compensation algorithm that modifies remaining weights.
training_free: Scores yes; compensation is a weight update
inference_native: YES if compensation skipped
metal_feasible: YES for scoring+deletion only
est_savings: SOTA claims for autoregressive LMs and image generators (with compensation)
notes: Same pattern as SlimLLM: usable scores, constraint-crossing recovery. Run score-only if adopted.

method: LLM-Pruner - REJECTED
mechanism: Gradient/Taylor saliency over coupled structure groups, then LoRA recovery fine-tune.
training_free: NO in practice - quality depends on LoRA recovery (training); gradient saliency also needs backward passes
inference_native: n/a
metal_feasible: NO - backward through u32-packed 1-bit MLX weights needs STE machinery we don't have; LoRA violates no-training rule outright
est_savings: 20% with recovery on FP models (reference only)
notes: Historically important, practically excluded. FLAP already beats it without any training.

method: PBS2P (Progressive Binarization with Semi-Structured Pruning) - FLAGGED, quantized-specific
mechanism: Post-training framework integrating binarization WITH semi-structured pruning; jointly optimizes binarization parameters (scales) to minimize combined pruning+quantization error; coarse-to-fine ratio search.
training_free: Post-training but optimizes binarization parameters on calibration data - calibration-based weight-value optimization
inference_native: Semi-structured (N:M-style) sparsity inside binary weights would need new Metal kernels; not width reduction
metal_feasible: NO without significant kernel work
est_savings: Beats binary PTQ baselines in ppl/accuracy (co-designed setting)
notes: CONSTRAINT-CROSSING and co-designed (it makes the binary model rather than pruning a frozen one). Its evidentiary value: binarized LLMs tolerate meaningful structured sparsity.

method: Sparse-BitNet - REJECTED (training-time) but key evidence
mechanism: Joint 1.58-bit quantization + dynamic N:M sparsification during training; finds 1.58-bit BitNet is NATURALLY MORE COMPATIBLE with N:M sparsity than full-precision models.
training_free: NO - training-time method
inference_native: n/a for us
metal_feasible: n/a
est_savings: n/a (reference)
notes: The headline finding is the useful part: width/sparsity redundancy survives extreme quantization, and extreme-quantized models may tolerate structured removal BETTER than FP ones. Supports the hypothesis behind width-pruning Bonsai-1bit; cite as motivation, not method.

method: Dynamic activation sparsity on group-quantized weights - orthogonal option
mechanism: Exploits per-input runtime activation sparsity: zigzag-patterned group-quantization layout + specialized sparse GEMV kernel + compact runtime index gathering. Weights entirely untouched.
training_free: YES - and perfectly weight-preserving (nothing deleted or changed)
inference_native: The quantized layout is what kernels consume, but requires reordering the packed layout and a new GEMV kernel
metal_feasible: PARTIAL - substantial Metal kernel work in our MLX fork (sparse GEMV + zigzag layout); more than 'modest'
est_savings: Up to 1.55x decode throughput; ZERO memory savings
notes: Not compression - a latency-only sibling. Park unless decode speed becomes the bottleneck; note the paper's warning that naive sparsity interacts badly with group-wise quantization (our g128 format), which also cautions any non-aligned width deletion.

method: GAP ANALYSIS + format-native synthesis for bonsai-fold
source: Synthesis of all searches (no direct prior art found for training-free width pruning of an already-1-bit pack; nearest works PBS2P/GQSA/Sparse-BitNet all co-design or train)
mechanism: The g128 affine 1-bit format defines the natural pruning units: (a) OUTPUT-row deletion (any linear) is byte-exact - drop the packed row + its scale/bias groups; (b) INPUT-dim deletion is byte-exact ONLY in 128-aligned bundles, else groups would mix weights under one shared scale/bias (a value change). Bonsai aligns perfectly: intermediate 17408 = 136 x 128 bundles per MLP; hidden 5120 = 40 x 128, so if head_dim=128, whole-head deletion (q/k/v rows + the head's aligned o_proj column-group) is byte-exact. Saliency per bundle = sum of per-channel scores.
training_free: YES by construction
inference_native: YES - pruned model is a standard smaller MLX quantized model; stock kernels, config-only changes (n_heads, intermediate_size), GQA ratio kept integral
metal_feasible: YES - likely zero kernel changes; only pack-surgery code (mirrors existing block-merge surgery)
est_savings: Stacked ceiling on the ~3.8 GB pack: MLP bundles 10-20% of ~2.4 GB MLP bytes (0.24-0.48 GB) + heads/attn-sublayers few % + vocab halving ~0.18 GB = plausible 0.4-0.7 GB on top of depth folding, all byte-exact
notes: Recommended recipe: FLAP fluctuation or SlimLLM-style holistic scores at 128-bundle granularity, DIET multi-domain voting, CoCurve-style interaction-aware joint selection via masked-forward KL (reuses Phase-1 harness), MultiPruner-style iterative depth+width budget. Publishable gap: nobody has shown training-free, byte-exact width pruning of a 1-bit pack. All damage numbers must be measured within-format (folded-1bit vs unfolded-1bit) per project rules.

method: Tile-level ANS lossless weight compression ("Approaching Shannon Bound with Lossless LLM Weight Compression")
mechanism: Asymmetric Numeral Systems entropy coding of weight tiles, with decompression aligned to GPU GEMM tiling so kernels consume the compressed stream on the fly (no dense materialization). Reported bit-rates within 0.01-0.1 bits of Shannon limit; works on bf16 down to int4/AWQ formats; finds effective entropy 2-10x below nominal bitwidth.
training_free: YES — lossless, zero weight-value change, no calibration. Fully satisfies constraint (1) and (4): surviving bytes decode bit-identically.
inference_native: YES — tile decode fused into the matmul path, not load-time decompression.
metal_feasible: No existing Metal/MLX port (CUDA/SGLang only). Port = ANS decode in threadgroup memory fused into our patched-MLX 1-bit dequant kernel; moderate effort, more than a table lookup but no new backend.
est_savings: On Bonsai 1-bit: sign bits are near max-entropy if +/- balanced, so gains concentrate in the f16 scale+bias metadata (~32 of 160 bits per g128 group). Realistic 4-12% total (~1.25 -> ~1.10-1.20 bpw); more only if sign words prove correlated.
notes: Best constraint fit of anything found: the ONLY family that is simultaneously training-free, inference-native, and weight-value-preserving. Cheap prerequisite: a census job measuring empirical entropy of Bonsai's u32 sign words and f16 scale/bias exponents would bound the payoff before any kernel work.

method: DFloat11 (Dynamic-Length Float)
mechanism: Huffman-codes the low-entropy exponent bits of BF16 weights (~11 bits effective, ~30% smaller); hierarchical LUTs in GPU SRAM + two-phase kernel + transformer-block-granularity decompression; outputs bit-for-bit identical to original.
training_free: YES — lossless, no calibration, no value change.
inference_native: YES — decode happens inside GPU kernels during inference (block-level, on the fly).
metal_feasible: CUDA only today; no Metal/MLX port found. The SRAM-LUT + two-phase scheme maps to Metal threadgroup memory; moderate effort. Simpler variant: apply the exponent-Huffman idea only to Bonsai's f16 scale/bias tensors.
est_savings: Format is BF16-specific, so direct reuse touches only our f16 group scales/biases (~0.25 of 1.25 bpw); ~30% of that slice = ~5-7% total model size.
notes: Strong existence proof that entropy-coded weights + direct-decode kernels are practical at generation-time throughput. Constraint-clean (lossless). Main limitation for us: our mass is in sign bits, not floats.

method: EntroLLM — entropy coding over already-quantized weights
mechanism: Huffman coding layered on existing uint4/uint8 PTQ weights plus a parallel segmented decoding strategy for weight retrieval at inference on edge GPUs (Jetson); 30% savings over uint8, 65% claim vs uint4 baselines; 32-147% faster on memory-limited devices.
training_free: YES for the coding stage — explicitly retraining-free, wraps an existing quantized model (the closest published analog to compressing an already-1-bit pack).
inference_native: Mostly — parallel segment decode at retrieval time; paper is vague on full fusion vs per-layer staging; flag for verification before relying on it.
metal_feasible: No Metal kernels; segmented-parallel Huffman decode is portable to Metal with moderate effort (similar shape to DFloat11 port).
est_savings: On 1-bit signs likely <5% unless Bonsai's sign stream is skewed/correlated; metadata slice same as DFloat11 (~5-7%). Their big ratios come from uint8/uint4 redundancy that a 1-bit format has already squeezed out.
notes: Useful as method template, not as drop-in: validates 'entropy-code an existing quantized pack, decode in kernel' on edge hardware. Constraint-clean if applied losslessly.

method: STBLLM — structured sign sparsity (N:M) for sub-1-bit binary LLMs
mechanism: Prunes binarized weights to per-layer N:M patterns using a Standardized Importance metric (weight magnitude x input feature norm) with Hessian-based salient/non-salient partitioning; non-salient regions get tailored re-binarization; 0.55 bpw at ppl 11.07 (3x better than BiLLM); custom CUDA sparse-tensor-core kernel.
training_free: PARTIAL — no gradient steps, but selection needs calibration activations/Hessian, and the non-salient-aware re-binarization RE-QUANTIZES surviving values. FLAG: crosses the never-alter-surviving-weights rule. A stripped variant (pure N:M sign deletion, scales refit closed-form) would be selection-only but is not what the paper evaluates.
inference_native: YES — sparse packed format consumed directly by their CUDA kernel.
metal_feasible: Unproven. Apple GPUs have no sparse tensor cores; a mask-guided binary GEMV in Metal is writable (modest-moderate), but N:M mask storage and gather overhead eat into gains at GEMV batch-1.
est_savings: Headline ~50% (1.1 -> 0.55 bpw). Realistic on Bonsai after mask overhead and no-FP-magnitudes handicap: ~25-35%, with real damage risk.
notes: Biggest practical blocker: SI metric needs FP magnitudes; our pack has only signs + scale/bias, so importance must come from activation statistics — calibration-based SELECTION (arguably allowed under 'selection is OK', but flag for Thanasis). Most relevant sub-1-bit paper for an already-binary model.

method: BTC-LLM — binary codebook over sign-vector clusters
mechanism: (a) learnable invertible scaling+rotation aligns binarized weights with FP distribution; (b) 'Flash Binary Codebook' clusters recurring binary vectors into compact indices (sign-based centroid updates), eliminating sparse masks; 0.7-1.11 bpw; 0.8-bit LLaMA-2-13B at -3.1% accuracy, 1.6x speedup vs FP16 on standard hardware.
training_free: NO — the transformation is gradient-optimized. FLAG. However, the codebook half alone (cluster g-length sign patterns from our existing u32 words, store indices) is runnable training-free on Bonsai — but assigning a centroid pattern to a group REPLACES its sign vector, so it is value-modifying; flag as constraint-crossing either way.
inference_native: YES — index -> codebook lookup at inference, no sparse-mask management; designed for standard hardware.
metal_feasible: No Metal port, but codebook-LUT dequant is the best-proven kernel class on Apple GPUs (llama.cpp IQ quants, EXL4 port). A g128-or-smaller sign-pattern LUT kernel in our MLX fork is modest effort.
est_savings: ~20-35% (1.125 -> ~0.8 bpw) IF sign patterns cluster; payoff is measurable in advance by clustering Bonsai's actual sign words offline.
notes: The codebook-only ablation is the interesting question for us: how much does it lose without the learnable transform? Paper doesn't isolate it favorably. Cheap offline experiment: histogram Bonsai's 32-bit sign words per layer — if the distribution is near-uniform, both codebook and entropy routes are dead.

method: NanoQuant — low-rank binary factorization, sub-1-bit
mechanism: W ~ s1 . (U+-1 V+-1^T) . s2 — two rank-r sign matrices plus channel scales; 0.55-1.0 bpw with all overheads (Llama-2-70B: 138 GB -> 5.75 GB); custom CUDA binary GEMV/GEMM consume packed format directly.
training_free: NO — 128-sample calibration, Hessian-aware preconditioning, ADMM init, block-wise reconstruction, scale refinement. FLAG: calibration-based optimization, and it requires the original FP weights, which do not exist for Bonsai (1-bit pack only).
inference_native: YES — packed binary factors consumed natively, no unpacking.
metal_feasible: No Metal port; binary GEMV is simple to write in Metal (modest), but moot given constraint failures.
est_savings: N/A for Bonsai — cannot be constructed from a 1-bit-only pack.
notes: Included for completeness as the 2026 sub-1-bit SOTA line; structurally inapplicable to this project.

method: QMoE — sub-1-bit dictionary-coded format with fused decode
source: arXiv 2310.16795 (Frantar & Alistarh; precedes 2024 window but foundational)
mechanism: GPTQ-ternarizes MoE experts then applies fixed-dictionary coding of natural sparsity, hitting <1 bpw on SwitchTransformer-scale MoEs; per-layer compressed format decoded by fused CUDA kernels at inference.
training_free: NO — GPTQ calibration modifies values. Also effectively ternary + MoE-specific; Bonsai is dense and the ternary arm is cut.
inference_native: YES — first published sub-1-bit direct-decode format.
metal_feasible: No; CUDA-only and MoE-structured. Not worth porting for a dense model.
est_savings: N/A for Bonsai.
notes: Historical anchor for 'sub-1-bit with native kernels is possible'; its gains ride on ternary zero-runs, which a dense balanced-sign 1-bit format lacks.

method: AQLM — additive multi-codebook vector quantization
mechanism: Sums of codebook vectors per group (~2-2.5 bpw effective); codebooks learned by gradient descent on calibration data plus end-to-end block fine-tuning; CUDA/Triton GPU kernels + Numba CPU.
training_free: NO — gradient-based codebook learning and fine-tuning. FLAG on both (1) and (4). Also requires FP weights (unavailable).
inference_native: YES on CUDA (codebook-lookup matvec kernels); no Metal/MLX kernels exist.
metal_feasible: Feasible in principle (LUT kernels port fine) but pointless here.
est_savings: NEGATIVE for Bonsai — AQLM's ~2 bpw landing zone is above our 1.125 bpw base; re-quantizing a 1-bit model through it is not meaningful.
notes: Listed because the task asked; verdict is clean rejection: fails training-free, needs FP source weights, and would enlarge the model.

method: QuIP# — E8 lattice codebook + incoherence processing
mechanism: Random Hadamard incoherence transform, then hardware-symmetric E8 lattice codebook at 2 bpw; calibration-based rounding plus fine-tuning for SOTA numbers; fast CUDA decode via codebook symmetry.
training_free: NO — calibration + fine-tuning; value-modifying; needs FP weights.
inference_native: YES on CUDA; no Metal kernels (its descendants — llama.cpp IQ formats — do have Metal kernels).
metal_feasible: Codebook decode: proven portable by the IQ-format lineage. Moot for construction reasons.
est_savings: NEGATIVE for Bonsai (2 bpw > 1.125 bpw base).
notes: Same structural rejection as AQLM. Relevant only as the intellectual ancestor of Metal-capable codebook kernels.

method: QTIP trellis quantization + EXL3/EXL4 Metal port
mechanism: Trellis-coded quantization with a procedural 'bitshift' codebook — decode is computed, not table-fetched, so ultra-high-dimensional codebooks cost no SRAM; EXL4 format port ships REAL Metal kernels (simdgroup_matrix GEMV + fast Walsh-Hadamard) on Apple Silicon at ~4 bpw.
training_free: NO — calibration-based construction (+optional fine-tuning); value-modifying; needs FP weights. FLAG.
inference_native: YES — and uniquely, Metal-native inference already EXISTS via the community port.
metal_feasible: PROVEN — the one codebook family with working Apple Silicon GPU kernels outside llama.cpp.
est_savings: N/A as compressor for Bonsai (lands at 2-4 bpw from FP weights).
notes: Value to us is purely as an engineering existence proof: procedural-codebook decode + Hadamard at decode-time run fine on M-series GPUs, derisking any custom LUT/trellis kernel we might add to the MLX fork.

method: llama.cpp IQ1_S / IQ1_M grid-codebook formats
mechanism: 1.5625 / 1.75 bpw grid/codebook formats descended from QuIP#-style lattices; construction requires an importance matrix ('result will be garbage' without) and codebook search with scale refits; production Metal, CUDA, CPU kernels.
training_free: NO — imatrix calibration drives codebook assignment and values are re-quantized. FLAG. Needs FP weights.
inference_native: YES — Metal kernels ship today (note: IQ decode was historically slow on Apple Silicon vs K-quants, discussion #5617).
metal_feasible: EXISTS — but in GGML, a different backend; porting just the dequant tables + matvec into our patched MLX fork would be modest.
est_savings: NEGATIVE — 1.5625 bpw > Bonsai's 1.125 bpw. Reference point only.
notes: Main takeaway: sub-2-bit codebook decode on Metal is production reality, but every such format sits ABOVE our current bpw. Nothing in the GGUF zoo goes below 1 bpw for binary weights.

method: Any-Precision LLM — bit-plane packed nested codebook
mechanism: Stores an 8-bit SqueezeLLM-style non-uniform quantized parent; lower precisions (3-7 bit) are prefixes of the bit-plane stack, one memory store serves all widths; custom CUDA GEMV reads bit-planes directly.
training_free: NO — parent codebook is Fisher-information-weighted k-means fit on calibration data (calibration-based optimization); value-modifying; needs FP weights.
inference_native: YES on CUDA (bit-plane GEMV).
metal_feasible: Portable in principle; moot.
est_savings: NONE for Bonsai — a 1-bit model is already the bottom bit-plane; there is no sub-plane to strip. The mechanism has no sub-1-bit analog.
notes: Task asked explicitly; verdict: category mismatch — it multiplexes precisions, it does not compress below the lowest one.

method: Ternary radix packing (llama.cpp TQ1_0 ~1.69 bpw; bitnet.cpp I2_S/TL1/TL2)
mechanism: Lossless radix repacking of ternary weights (5 trits per byte etc.) with LUT-based CPU mpGEMM kernels (ARM incl. Apple CPUs via NEON; Metal support absent/limited).
training_free: YES (pure repacking) — but doubly out of scope: the ternary arm was cut 2026-07-28, and the mechanism does not transfer.
inference_native: YES on CPU; not on Metal.
metal_feasible: Would need new kernels; irrelevant.
est_savings: ZERO for Bonsai — binary weights have no radix slack: 1 bit per sign IS the packing floor. Sub-1-bit for a binary model can only come from sparsity, codebooks, or entropy coding (rows above).
notes: Included to close out the 'sub-1-bit packing of binary/ternary' bullet: the ternary trick (log2(3)=1.585<2) has no binary analog.

method: SeedLM — LFSR pseudo-random seed reconstruction
mechanism: Per-block seed drives an LFSR generating a random basis; block ~ linear combo with a few stored coefficients; 3-4 bpw; data-free; trades compute for memory traffic; FPGA demo ~4x over FP16.
training_free: YES — explicitly data-free and calibration-free (rare!). But value-modifying (approximation) — FLAG on (4) — and fitting seeds needs the original FP weights, so it cannot be applied to the 1-bit pack.
inference_native: YES in concept (regenerate-in-kernel); only FPGA implementation published, no GPU/Metal kernels.
metal_feasible: Plausible (Apple authorship; LFSR + small GEMM per block is Metal-friendly) but nothing exists; and 3-4 bpw is far above our base.
est_savings: NEGATIVE for Bonsai.
notes: Conceptually interesting neighbor (training-free compression with compute-for-memory trade) but wrong operating point and wrong input format for this project.

method: Q-Palette — fractional-bit quantizer suite (trellis/vector/scalar)
mechanism: Family of fractional-bit quantizers (trellis-coded near distortion-optimal down through fast scalar) with optimized CUDA kernels across bitwidths; mixed-scheme per-layer bit allocation; ~36% faster decoding vs NF baselines.
training_free: NO — weight-only PTQ with calibration; value-modifying; needs FP weights.
inference_native: YES on CUDA; no Metal.
metal_feasible: Kernels portable with effort (trellis decode proven on Metal via EXL4 port); moot for construction reasons.
est_savings: N/A — operating range ~2-4 bpw, above our base.
notes: Reference for what fractional-bit kernel engineering looks like in 2025; rejected on the same three grounds as AQLM/QuIP#/QTIP.

method: Sublayer-granular dropping (MHA and MLP pruned independently): BlockPruner / FinerCut / data-free attention-layer pruning
source: BlockPruner arXiv:2406.10594 (ACL Findings 2025); FinerCut arXiv:2405.18218; 'Data-Free Pruning of Self-Attention Layers in LLMs' arXiv:2512.20636 (Dec 2025); He et al. 'Not All Attention Is Needed'
mechanism: Treat each block's attention sublayer and MLP sublayer as separate deletion candidates instead of dropping whole transformer blocks. Selection via perplexity/KL on calibration text (BlockPruner: iterative greedy; FinerCut: output-change minimization; 2512.20636: fully data-free identity-similarity criterion). Residual stream makes removal a pure module skip.
training_free: YES. Deletion-only; selection uses calibration text (or none for the data-free variant). No gradients, no weight updates.
inference_native: YES. Surviving weights byte-identical, format untouched; MLX just skips the module (same as existing block-drop operator, finer granularity).
metal_feasible: Trivial — no kernel changes at all; config/module-list edit in the MLX model class.
est_savings: Attention sublayer of Bonsai ~16 MB/block vs ~54 MB for a whole block (MLP ~38 MB). FinerCut reports 42% of attention sublayers removable in Llama3-70B at ~99% performance without fine-tuning; mid/late-layer attention is the most redundant. Plausibly 300-600 MB on the ~3.8 GB pack beyond whole-block budget at equal damage.
notes: Best single fit for bonsai-fold that a whole-block-only sweep would miss: adds 'drop-attn' / 'drop-mlp' operators orthogonal to the H4 merges. Fully value-preserving. Caveat: dropping attention changes KV-cache layout per layer (must keep DSpark drafter disabled, already project policy).

method: EvoPress-style evolutionary search over per-block compression profiles
source: EvoPress arXiv:2410.14649 (ICML 2025, IST-DASLab, code: github.com/IST-DASLab/EvoPress); GeLaCo arXiv:2507.10059 (evolutionary layer-collapse search with module-wise similarity fitness, Pareto frontier over compression x quality)
mechanism: Search (evolutionary, low sample complexity, provable convergence) over which blocks to drop / which spans to merge / which tensors get which format, scored on a small calibration set. Key empirical finding: per-layer error is NOT monotonic or additive — profiles with lower summed per-layer error can be worse end-to-end, so greedy/one-shot metric ranking (BI, cosine, per-block KL) is provably suboptimal.
training_free: YES. Pure configuration search; weights untouched. Calibration data used only for scoring candidates.
inference_native: YES. Output is just a drop/merge profile executed by existing operators.
metal_feasible: Yes — it is a driver loop around existing MLX eval; fits the 2h-job constraint if generations are batched and fitness uses cheap KL on short sequences.
est_savings: No new bytes by itself; EvoPress reports state-of-the-art quality at fixed drop budgets vs metric-ranked dropping — i.e., more blocks removable at the same damage threshold.
notes: Directly reusable to co-optimize the joint space bonsai-fold already has (drop + sign-election merge + promotion merge per span). GeLaCo is the closest published relative of the H4 merge search. Counterpoint worth reading first: arXiv:2604.24938 below.

method: Calibration-configuration dominance in depth pruning (methodology result)
source: 'Rethinking Layer Redundancy: Calibration Matters More Than Search in LLM Depth Pruning' arXiv:2604.24938 (2026)
mechanism: Empirical study across LLM families: the calibration data configuration (domain, length, amount) changes which layers look redundant far more than the choice of search/importance algorithm; under fixed calibration, simple one-shot selection converges to what complex searches find.
training_free: YES (analysis of training-free pipelines).
inference_native: N/A — methodology, not a compressor.
metal_feasible: N/A.
est_savings: Indirect: better drop-set choice at zero added compute by diversifying calibration text before investing in fancier search.
notes: Cheap, immediately actionable check for the existing on-policy vs off-policy KL chains: sweep calibration domain/length before trusting any block ranking. Tension with EvoPress's claim that search matters — worth one controlled experiment on Bonsai.

method: Vocabulary trimming: delete unused/rare token rows from 1-bit embedding and lm_head
source: VocabTrim arXiv:2506.22694; SqueezeBits 'Vocabulary Trimming' blog (blog.squeezebits.com/vocabulary-trimming-methods); VocabTailor arXiv:2508.15229; Compact arXiv:2509.06836
mechanism: Vocab 248,320 is multilingual-sized; token frequencies are Zipfian and 'dead' tokens (unused scripts/languages) never fire.
