Delete their rows from the quantized embedding and lm_head, remap token ids in tokenizer + config. Row deletion respects g128 packing (groups run along the 5120 hidden dim within a row), so surviving rows are byte-identical.
training_free: YES. Pure row selection/deletion from corpus token statistics; no weight values touched.
inference_native: YES. Smaller lookup table and smaller logits GEMM — strictly faster decode (lm_head is memory-bound at 248k vocab).
metal_feasible: Trivial — smaller tensors, zero kernel changes. Tokenizer remap is pure Python.
est_savings: Embed + lm_head = 2 x 248,320 x 5120 = 2.54B params ≈ 9.4% of the 27B ≈ ~358 MB at 1.125 bpw. Trimming 60-70% of vocab (English-centric eval) saves ~215-250 MB (~6% of pack) plus decode speedup.
notes: This is the 'orthogonal axis' item in pending task #10. Caveats: (a) OOV text degrades unless byte-fallback tokens are kept — always keep byte/ASCII tokens and special tokens; (b) folded-vs-unfolded comparisons must use the same trimmed tokenizer on both sides to stay within-format; (c) token-frequency census over the eval corpora is a cheap first experiment.

method: Structured width pruning of MLP intermediate channels in multiples of 128
source: FLAP (arXiv:2312.11983, AAAI 2024, retraining-free structured pruning); Compact arXiv:2509.06836 (joint vocab + FFN-channel pruning); Wanda arXiv:2306.11695 (importance = |W| x activation norm); 'Function-Aware Neuron Grouping' arXiv:2512.23014
mechanism: Rank the 17,408 MLP intermediate channels per block by activation-aware importance (calibration forward passes only); delete lowest channels as whole rows of up/gate projections and matching columns of down_proj. Deleting in multiples of 128 keeps down_proj's g128 input-dim groups intact so surviving groups stay byte-identical (rows of up/gate are trivially safe).
training_free: YES if selection-only (Wanda/FLAP-style scoring). FLAP's optional bias compensation is a closed-form weight edit — skip it or FLAG it.
inference_native: YES. Just smaller K/N dims; MLX quantized matmul handles any K that is a multiple of the group size.
metal_feasible: Yes, no kernel change if deletions are 128-aligned on the down_proj input dim; otherwise a repack (byte-level shuffle, value-preserving) is needed.
est_savings: MLP = 3 x 5120 x 17408 per block ≈ 65% of block bytes. Pruning 12.5% of channels (2176 = 17 groups of 128) model-wide ≈ 8% of MLP bytes ≈ ~250 MB, tunable per block (combine with per-block KL sensitivity).
notes: Second orthogonal axis in task #10. Interacts with depth ops: width-prune the blocks you keep, drop the ones you don't. Attention head pruning is the same idea but collides with RoPE/GQA layout — check Bonsai head config in the census first.

method: LaCo layer-collapse merging (prior art for the promotion merge family)
source: LaCo arXiv:2402.11187 ('Reserving-Differences-while-Seeking-Common'); MKA (manifold-based knowledge alignment merging, arXiv:2405.16039 family)
mechanism: Collapse a span of consecutive layers into one by folding parameter differences of later layers into an anchor layer (closed-form weight arithmetic), candidate spans chosen by representation similarity.
training_free: YES (closed-form merge, similarity-based selection).
inference_native: Only if the merged result is representable in a native format. Raw delta-addition of two g128-affine 1-bit tensors yields up to 4 values per position — exactly the regime bonsai-fold's 2-bit promotion merge formalizes. Generic FP averaging/LaCo output is NOT 1-bit-representable → requantization → FLAG.
metal_feasible: Promotion-merge variant already runs in the project's patched MLX; generic LaCo would need dense fallback (out of scope).
est_savings: Same as block dropping per collapsed span, with lower damage than deletion on mid-depth spans (LaCo: ~25-30% layer reduction keeping most benchmark performance on Llama-2).
notes: Mainly useful as citable prior art positioning H4's sign-election/promotion merges; MKA's similarity-based span selection is a drop-in alternative candidate generator. FLAG any variant that leaves the closed-form/native-format rules.

method: ReplaceMe: replace a pruned block span with a closed-form linear transform
mechanism: Estimate a single linear map (least squares / optimal transport on calibration activations) approximating the removed span's residual update, then fold it into an adjacent projection matrix. Up to ~25% depth pruning retaining ~90% performance, no training.
training_free: YES in their sense (closed-form estimation, no gradients) — but it is calibration-based construction of new weight values.
inference_native: FLAG. Folding the map into a surviving 1-bit tensor requires requantization (breaks byte-identical rule). Keeping it as a standalone f16 5120x5120 matrix is value-preserving for survivors but costs 52.4 MB — roughly one whole block's bytes — so it only pays when one LT replaces a multi-block span (2+ blocks ≈ 108+ MB).
metal_feasible: Standalone-LT variant: trivial (one extra dense matmul in MLX). Folded variant: no.
est_savings: Net ~54 MB per (2-block span → 1 LT), scaling with span length; damage reportedly much lower than bare dropping at equal depth removed.
notes: Report FLAGGED: constraint-crossing under the strict 'no calibration-based weight construction' reading, even though gradient-free. If ever allowed, the standalone-LT form preserves all surviving weights byte-identically and slots in as a third operator besides drop and merge.

method: EoRA: training-free low-rank compensation of compression damage
mechanism: Project the output error introduced by compression (here: block drops/merges) onto the eigenspace of input activations and derive closed-form low-rank adapters (minutes, small calibration set, no gradients) that are added in parallel to surviving layers. Recovers e.g. +4-11 points on reasoning tasks for aggressively compressed Llama models.
training_free: YES (SVD/eigendecomposition only, no fine-tuning) — but adapters are new calibration-derived parameters; original weights untouched.
inference_native: YES. Extra rank-r f16 matmul alongside the 1-bit matmul; MLX expresses this natively (LoRA-style path).
metal_feasible: Trivial — standard dense ops, no kernel work.
est_savings: NEGATIVE bytes: rank-64 pair on one 5120x5120 linear ≈ 1.3 MB f16. Buys damage headroom that converts into 1-3 extra droppable blocks (~54-160 MB net) if compensation recovers enough KL.
notes: FLAG for project-rule review: it does not alter surviving weights (letter of the rule holds) but adds calibration-derived parameters, which brushes against 'no calibration-based weight updates'. Cleanest use: compensate only merged/dropped spans and report with/without.

method: Double quantization of the g128 scale/bias metadata (k-quant superblock trick)
source: QLoRA double quantization arXiv:2305.14314; llama.cpp k-quants (6-bit sub-scales + per-superblock f16, github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp tools/quantize); EntroLLM arXiv:2505.02380
mechanism: The f16 scale+bias per 128 weights is the pack's overhead (0.125-0.25 bpw of the 1.125 bpw effective — i.e., 11-20% of all bytes). Quantize scales/biases to 8 bits per group with one f16 meta-scale per superblock of 16-32 groups, exactly as GGUF k-quants do.
training_free: YES, data-free (pure rounding of existing metadata).
inference_native: YES with a modest kernel change: one extra multiply in the dequant path of the patched MLX 1-bit kernel.
metal_feasible: Yes — small, localized edit to the existing fork's dequant inner loop; k-quants prove the pattern on every backend.
est_savings: Halves metadata: ~5-10% of total pack bytes (~200-400 MB region on a 3.8 GB pack) with typically negligible quality cost at 8-bit scales.
notes: FLAGGED value-modifying: dequantized weight values shift slightly (scale rounding), violating byte-identical weight preservation. Within-format damage is measurable with the existing KL harness. The single biggest 'deployment-format community' trick applicable to this pack.

method: Lossless entropy coding of weight planes with on-the-fly decode (DFloat11 / EntroLLM / ZipNN family)
source: DFloat11 arXiv:2504.11651 (NeurIPS 2025, github.com/LeanModels/DFloat11); EntroLLM arXiv:2505.02380; ZipNN (Hershcovitch et al. 2025); ECF8 (Yang et al. 2025)
mechanism: Entropy-code low-entropy weight representations (BF16 exponents, skewed quantized codes) and decode inside the inference kernel (custom CUDA Huffman/LUT decoders). ~30% lossless for BF16 models.
training_free: YES, lossless variants are perfectly value-preserving.
inference_native: On CUDA yes; on Metal NO — no such kernels exist for MLX, and a warp-cooperative Huffman decoder is beyond 'modest kernel changes'. ZipNN is load-time decompress-to-dense → violates constraint (2) outright (disk-only benefit).
metal_feasible: Not today; substantial Metal kernel project.
est_savings: Near zero on the dominant plane anyway: 1-bit sign planes of a trained model are near-maximum entropy (see Sign Lock-In below), so only the f16 scale/bias sidecar compresses — maybe 20-40% of the 11-20% metadata share ≈ 2-8% of pack, before kernel cost.
notes: Mostly EXCLUDED by constraints (2)/(3). One free by-product worth doing: a cheap entropy census of Bonsai's sign planes and scale/bias planes (gzip/zstd ratio per tensor) to (a) confirm signs are incompressible, (b) detect any exactly duplicated scale/bias patterns that could be deduped losslessly at file level.

method: Sign Lock-In: sign planes bottleneck sub-bit compression (negative result, saves effort)
source: arXiv:2602.17063 (Feb 2026); QMoE arXiv:2310.16795 as the contrasting case
mechanism: Evidence that trained weight-sign configurations persist from random init and are statistically near-incompressible — the sign plane is the irreducible object 1-bit formats store. QMoE's sub-1-bit dictionary coding only works because sparse MoE experts have hyper-compressible (near-zero-dominated) quantized weights; dense Bonsai does not.
training_free: N/A (analysis).
inference_native: N/A.
metal_feasible: N/A.
est_savings: Zero — its value is ruling out the 'entropy-code the sign bits' direction for a dense 1-bit model before anyone spends a week on it.
notes: Below 1 bit/weight on this model, the only honest levers are structural (fewer weights: depth, width, vocab) or metadata (scales) — which is precisely bonsai-fold's thesis. Good citation for the paper's related-work section.

method: SeedLM: weights as LFSR pseudo-random seeds + closed-form coefficients
mechanism: Per weight block, search an LFSR seed whose generated basis, linearly combined with a few quantized coefficients (least squares, data-free), reconstructs the block; kernels regenerate weights on the fly, trading compute for memory traffic. 3-4 bpw on Llama-3 70B at parity with calibration methods.
training_free: YES (data-free, closed-form).
inference_native: In principle (FPGA demos); no Metal/MLX kernels exist — LFSR-regeneration matmul is a new kernel family, more than a modest change.
metal_feasible: Not without significant kernel work, ironically despite being Apple research.
est_savings: Not applicable at 1.125 bpw base: SeedLM targets 3-4 bpw from FP16; approximating existing 1-bit sign planes with sub-1-bit seeds would be severe lossy re-approximation. Only conceivable niche: compressing the f16 scale sidecar (~unexplored).
notes: FLAGGED value-modifying and effectively EXCLUDED for this base model; included because it is the one Apple-native 'exotic format' a Metal-focused reviewer will ask about.

method: Cross-layer weight sharing / shared-basis reconstruction (MASA, Basis Sharing, DeltaLLM)
source: MASA arXiv:2508.04581; Basis Sharing (ICLR 2025, openreview.net/forum?id=gp32jvUquq); DeltaLLM arXiv:2501.18596; 'Cross-layer Attention Sharing' arXiv:2408.01890
mechanism: Represent many layers' matrices as combinations of shared dictionary atoms / SVD bases (+ per-layer coefficients or low-rank deltas), storing the shared part once.
training_free: MASA/Basis Sharing: gradient-free decomposition but calibration-derived and value-modifying. DeltaLLM: requires training the deltas → fails constraint (1) outright.
inference_native: NO for a 1-bit pack: reconstruction produces dense FP weights (decompress-to-dense at runtime) and the shared-basis product cannot be expressed in the g128 1-bit format.
metal_feasible: No native path; would need a new kernel family plus dense intermediates.
est_savings: Papers claim 20-50% on FP models; effectively 0 available here.
notes: EXCLUDED on constraints (1)/(2). The only surviving relative is exact dedup: if any two quantized tensors are byte-identical (e.g., after merges), store once and alias in safetensors — lossless, trivially native, but expected hit rate ~0 outside deliberate ties.

method: Tied / shared embedding-unembedding and per-tensor format mixing (deployment-community tricks)
source: ExecuTorch use_shared_embedding + 4-bit g32 embedding quant (docs.pytorch.org/executorch, examples/models/llama); llama.cpp --token-embedding-type / --leave-output-tensor / k-quant mixes; MLX mixed_2_6-style quant_predicate recipes (github.com/ml-explore/mlx-examples PR#1132)
mechanism: (a) Tie lm_head to the embedding table and store once; (b) give embedding/lm_head/first/last blocks different formats than the trunk via per-tensor format predicates.
training_free: (a) YES mechanically, but Bonsai's embed and lm_head are presumably not weight-tied, so tying = replacing one with the other → value-modifying FLAG and likely large damage; worth a one-line census check for near-duplication first. (b) YES — but only promotion (more bits) is possible from a 1-bit base, which grows the pack.
inference_native: YES for both — MLX QuantizedEmbedding already supports as_linear reuse (tied path), and per-tensor formats are native.
metal_feasible: Trivial.
est_savings: (a) ~179 MB (one full 248k x 5120 1-bit matrix) IF tables were tied/near-identical — must verify with a cosine/byte census before believing; (b) zero-to-negative bytes, quality lever only.
notes: The census (embed vs lm_head similarity, per-row norms) is a 10-minute job on existing tooling and settles (a) definitively. If Bonsai shipped untied (likely for a 27B), record the negative result and move on.

method: Depth pruning harms test-time scaling / long CoT disproportionately (evaluation caveat)
source: 'When Fewer Layers Break More Chains' arXiv:2510.22228 (Oct 2025)
mechanism: Empirical: layer-pruned models degrade far more on long chain-of-thought and test-time-scaling regimes than on short-form benchmarks; damage is invisible to perplexity/short-KL metrics.
training_free: N/A (evaluation finding).
inference_native: N/A.
metal_feasible: N/A.
est_savings: None — it caps how much depth removal survives honest evaluation.
notes: Directly relevant because project policy runs Bonsai with thinking mode ON: the anchor mini-bench should include at least one long-reasoning task, or the KL-chain results will overstate how many blocks are safely droppable. Cheap to add to the existing mini-bench chain.

method: Retraining-based recovery after pruning (perimeter marker: excluded)
source: 'A Free Lunch in LLM Compression: Revisiting Retraining after Pruning' arXiv:2510.14444; 'Reassessing Layer Pruning in LLMs' (2024); Minitron/Puzzle/Nemotron line (NVIDIA)
mechanism: All post-2025 SOTA depth-compression numbers that beat training-free methods do it via cheap retraining/distillation after pruning.
training_free: NO — categorically excluded by constraint (1).
notes: Listed only to mark the sweep perimeter: when comparing bonsai-fold results against literature, filter out these hybrids or the training-free numbers will look artificially weak. Also excluded on the same ground: SliceGPT/SVD-LLM/ASVD/CALDERA (calibration-optimized weight rewrites, dense outputs incompatible with the 1-bit format).
